pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, answered about their own codebase with concrete examples; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through your milestones. What does 'this milestone is done' mean, and what did you do when one turned out to be too big?
expected_points: every milestone leaves the project runnable and green (go test -race ./... passes), not just green at the end
done means the milestone's acceptance criterion holds and the behaviour can be run, not 'as good as I can make it'
an oversized milestone gets split, with the already-working part shipped and ticked
the walking skeleton came first: thinnest end-to-end slice, to retire integration risk and get feedback loops working on day one

questions.prompt: Draw your import graph. Which package may import which, and what would it take to swap your storage for a different implementation?
expected_points: dependencies point inward: the domain package imports none of their other packages; storage and transport import it
main is a composition root — wiring only, no rules, because it is the code tests cannot reach
the seam is a small interface declared by the consumer, so swapping storage is a new package plus one line in main
internal/ marks what is not promised to outside callers; no util/common/helpers packages

questions.prompt: The harness requires 60% statement coverage. Why is that a floor and not a goal, and how would you tell an honest suite from one written to hit the number?
expected_points: below the floor whole packages are unexercised and 'the tests pass' means little
above it the number stops carrying information — high coverage of trivia with low coverage of decision logic is a worse suite
chasing the number turns a measure into a target (assert-nothing tests, testing getters)
honest tests pin named behaviour at package boundaries; each one would catch something real breaking

questions.prompt: Show me one wrapped error and one context in your code. Why is the error wrapped that way, and where does cancellation actually stop work?
expected_points: wrap with %w plus what was being attempted, so callers keep errors.Is/As matching
sentinel errors at package boundaries give callers something to match on
handle or return, never both; main turns errors into exit codes or responses
context is the first parameter, passed down to anything that can block, never stored in a struct
they can name the call that observes cancellation, or explain honestly that the work is not cancellable

questions.prompt: Which of your ADRs held up under the build, which did you revise, and what did reality tell you that you didn't know when you wrote it?
expected_points: a specific decision that held, with the evidence that it held
a specific decision that changed, superseded by a new ADR rather than edited in place
the old ADR's status is updated to point at the one that replaced it
revising a decision under evidence is the point of the format, not a failure of planning

questions.prompt: Point at something you deliberately did not build or did not abstract. How did you decide?
expected_points: the milestone's acceptance criteria are the definition of done
non-goals from the PRD win by default; breaking one takes an ADR
rule of three — abstract on the third occurrence, not the first; one implementation and no test double means indirection, not flexibility
hard-code configuration until a second caller exists

questions.prompt: For every goroutine in your project: what does it own, who waits for it, and how does it stop? If there are none, why not?
expected_points: each goroutine has a clear owner, a waiter (WaitGroup, channel, errgroup-style join) and a stop signal
no goroutine outlives the thing that started it without a documented reason
'sequential is fast enough at the sizes in my PRD' is a strong answer when backed by the expected workload
the race detector is part of the normal test command, not a pre-review ceremony
